stories.headline: Dems seize on midterm rout to demand ICE reform, but polls reveal a twist in who prioritized immigration
stories.note: Democrats are reading their midterm wins as an immigration mandate, but Fox polling shows their own voters (3%) and Hispanic voters (15%) barely ranked immigration as a priority, while 27% of Republicans did.
body: Fresh off their midterm sweep, Democrats, led by a group of newly elected Texas members, are pressing for immigration reform and warning would-be 2028 presidential candidates that it must be at the top of their agenda.

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who ousted GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in a redrawn South Texas district, said anyone seeking the group's support in 2028 "has to prioritize immigration reform, period." Pulido ran mainly on affordability.

The polling tells a different story. Fox News Digital polling found 27% of Republican voters named immigration their top issue, compared with just 3% of Democrats. Among Hispanic voters, the Fox News Voter Poll found 45% put the economy first, 26% the state of democracy and only 15% immigration, with nearly identical numbers in Texas.

Rep. Henry Cuellar and UnidosUS's Texas director Eric Holguín both pointed to cost of living as the main driver, and analyst Henry Olsen of the Ethics and Public Policy Center said the vote looked more like a rejection of Trump than enthusiasm for Democratic policies. Holguín warned Democrats that Latino voters are watching whether they deliver.

RNC press secretary Natalie Baldassarre said President Trump is keeping his promise to secure the border, adding that Republicans remain focused on affordability while Democrats fight among themselves and focus on impeachment.

Why it matters: If Democrats treat a cost-of-living protest vote as a green light to roll back border enforcement, they risk misreading their own coalition, giving Republicans an opening to own the issue that their base still ranks number one.

stories.headline: Dems' California redistricting mastermind flips script after helping party win 5 GOP seats: 'Kill'
stories.note: The man who drew California's Democrat-friendly Prop 50 map, which flipped five GOP seats, now wants to 'kill partisan gerrymandering' after his side cashed in, a glaring display of Democratic hypocrisy.
body: Paul Mitchell, the data consultant behind California's Proposition 50 congressional map, is now calling for an end to partisan gerrymandering across the country, just after his map helped Democrats flip all five Republican-held seats it targeted.

In a San Francisco Chronicle op-ed published Wednesday, Mitchell urged lawmakers to "kill partisan gerrymandering for good" and said the incoming Congress should set national standards for drawing districts. Voters approved Prop 50 in November 2025, swapping the state's independent maps for a Democratic-friendly map through 2030.

Mitchell admitted Prop 50 was built to help Democrats, but he defended it as a temporary answer to Texas Republicans' redistricting. He told Fox News Digital the timing wasn't meant to line up with anyone's plans and said he had always intended to speak out once the election ended.

He also argued Republicans, having "lost in this war," might now be more open to reform. He wants Congress to ban mid-decade redistricting and says independent commissions in every state would be the best fix. However, he expects California's Prop 50 maps to stay in place through 2030.
By contrast, outgoing Georgia Republican Gov. Brian Kemp said he would not call a special session to redraw maps or limit his successor's powers before leaving office.

Why it matters: Democrats gerrymandered their way to extra seats and are now calling for a truce while keeping their gains locked in. Republicans can point to that as proof that Democrats' 'fair maps' talk only applies after they've won.

stories.headline: Democrats eye killing Senate filibuster, and lawmaker warns move could be a 'double-edged sword'
stories.note: Incoming Senate Democrats are openly floating nuking the filibuster, the power grab Republicans warned about, while even one of their own cautions it could backfire.
body: As they prepare to take control of the Senate, Democratic senators are signaling that eliminating the 60-vote filibuster is on the table.

Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts told Fox News Digital the filibuster "has to be on the table," and Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who launched a challenge to Chuck Schumer for majority leader on Thursday, has called it "anti-democratic." However, he said the caucus would need to discuss how to proceed.

Not everyone is on board. Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey called the idea potentially "a double-edged sword." He urged colleagues to be clear-eyed about the consequences and to try passing legislation through other means first.

Schumer stayed silent when asked whether he'd back ending the filibuster if Democrats also win the White House in 2028. Ending the 60-vote rule would let a simple majority pass most bills, which would also hand Republicans the same power whenever they regain control.

The article notes that President Trump had urged Senate Republicans to scrap the filibuster to pass the SAVE America Act, warning that Democrats would get rid of it themselves once they won the majority.

Why it matters: Trump's warning is coming true. Democrats' openness to scrapping a longstanding Senate guardrail gives Republicans a clear message about overreach, and Kim's warning shows the party is divided on it.

stories.headline: Small town residents cry for help as immigrant influx fueled by trucking industry has unintended consequences
stories.note: Fox's on-the-ground look at southwest Ohio backs the GOP's push for tougher immigration and commercial trucking enforcement, highlighting a five-day crackdown that produced 36 arrests, 31 of them on immigration-related charges.
body: In the third part of a Fox News Digital series, residents of southwest Ohio describe how a fast-growing Uzbek immigrant community tied to the trucking industry has left them worried about safety on local roads and in their neighborhoods.

At a Nov. 4 Hamilton Township trustees meeting, dozens of residents raised concerns about alleged trucking fraud, crowded schools, crime and a planned mosque. In nearby Middletown, Fox visited an abandoned former restaurant that is registered as the headquarters of a trucking company with more than two dozen safety violations.

Police Chief Quillan Short shared results from a coordinated freight-fraud crackdown held Oct. 19-23: 561 traffic stops, 258 truck inspections, 423 citations, 73 vehicles and 49 drivers placed out of service, and 36 arrests, 31 of them tied to immigration-related offenses. Trustee Darryl Cordrey called the numbers "staggering" and said Biden-era immigration policies contributed to the problem.

Republican state Rep. Michelle Teska is pushing a bill to tighten commercial driver licensing, including requiring English-language driver exams. She noted that Ohio currently offers CDL and driver's license tests in 10 languages. Nationally, federal regulators have placed about 34,000 drivers out of service for failing English-proficiency rules and revoked or canceled over 31,000 illegally issued CDLs.
The local Uzbek association said in a statement that it recognizes residents' concerns and wants to work with the community through open dialogue.

Why it matters: The story puts real local consequences behind the GOP's argument for stricter immigration and trucking enforcement, and it shows the Trump administration's CDL crackdown and Republican state lawmakers responding to what residents are reporting.

stories.headline: Florida Republican on Democrats' strategy: 'That's the choice they have to make ... persecution or policy'
stories.note: Rep. Randy Fine, who grew his margin to 19 points despite the blue wave, argues the GOP doesn't need new policies, just a fighting posture under Jim Jordan, and predicts Democrats will overreach on 'persecution.'
body: Florida Rep. Randy Fine says House Republicans heading into the minority should stop worrying about compromise and start fighting, and he believes new minority leader Jim Jordan is the right person to lead that effort.

Fine, who expanded his own victory margin from 14 points to 19 even as the GOP lost the House, told Fox News Digital that voters punished Republicans not for their policies but because they didn't see the party fighting for them. He called Jordan both the conference's best fighter and an extraordinary communicator.

He said Jordan's job will be to push back on impeachments and investigations and to explain why Democratic proposals like Medicare-for-all won't help people. He expects the most likely result to be gridlock: Democrats pass bills, Trump vetoes them, and Republicans sustain the vetoes.

Fine said he is open to compromise only if Republicans get real wins, such as voter ID or less immigration. He also named Sen. John Fetterman and Reps. Jared Moskowitz and Josh Gottheimer as Democrats he'd gladly work with on foreign policy.

His bottom line for Democrats: voters didn't elect them for vengeance. He summed up their options as "Persecution or policy," predicting they'll choose persecution and pay for it in two years, just as Republicans did.
Why it matters: Fine is laying out a comeback plan for the GOP: unite behind Jordan, block Democratic overreach, and let Democrats' focus on investigations become the issue in 2028.

stories.headline: Inside the DSA campaign to destroy 'ultra-Zionists' Schumer and Jeffries
stories.note: The NY Post reports that Democratic Socialists are organizing to strip Schumer and Jeffries of their leadership posts and take their seats, a sign of a deepening Democratic civil war right after the midterms.
body: Members of the Democratic Socialists of America are organizing a campaign against Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the two top congressional Democrats from New York, according to posts on a members-only DSA discussion board reviewed by The Post.

The plan calls for flooding members of Congress with letters and calls to oppose both men for leadership, followed by efforts to replace them with socialists in 2028. The national DSA's "Say No to Schumer" campaign has already generated more than 6,000 letters, and members want the group's eight elected officials to oppose both men or demand concessions.

The rhetoric is harsh. One DSA leader called both men "corporate shills," and other members labeled them "ultra-Zionists" and "ghouls." Others argued that a weak Speaker Jeffries might actually help their cause.

Schumer is already under pressure, with 10 senators or senators-elect, including Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin, saying they'll vote against him and Chris Van Hollen challenging him. Jeffries has backing from AOC, NY AG Letitia James and Mayor Zohran Mamdani. A source said James had warned DSA to back off. Schumer and Jeffries declined to comment.
The Post also reports that a DSA member said the Sunrise Movement was paying people to fly to Washington to protest at Schumer's office, where Sunrise said more than 50 young people were arrested.

Why it matters: Democrats' new majorities haven't even been sworn in, and the party's socialist wing is already turning on its own leaders. That kind of infighting gives Republicans an opening and could weaken Democratic unity in the next Congress.

stories.headline: President Trump rips Gavin Newsom's death row decision as 'disaster for Justice in America'
stories.note: Trump is hammering likely 2028 Democratic contender Gavin Newsom for commuting all 548 California death sentences, a move that has outraged victims' families and prosecutors and handed the GOP a potent tough-on-crime issue.
body: President Trump blasted California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Saturday for commuting the death sentences of all 548 inmates on the state's death row, calling it "a disaster for Justice in America" in a Truth Social post.

Trump called Newsom "incompetent and insensitive" for not letting the legal process run its course, said victims' families are rightly devastated, and expressed hope that the decision will be overturned.

Victims' relatives are furious. Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was kidnapped and murdered in 1993, said Newsom is moving some of the worst killers closer to freedom. Her killer, Richard Allen Davis, was sentenced to death in 1996.

Prosecutors are also fighting back. Former DA Anne Marie Schubert of the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation plans a court challenge and said clemency "is not a rubber stamp." Orange County DA Todd Spitzer is asking the state Supreme Court to block the commutations, which state law requires the court to approve for repeat felons.

Newsom said he respects those who disagree, including victims' families, but called state-sanctioned killing incompatible with California's values. California hasn't executed anyone since 2006, and Newsom imposed a moratorium in 2019.

Why it matters: Newsom is widely seen as a 2028 White House hopeful, and a blanket commutation for hundreds of convicted murderers gives Republicans a clear, emotional tough-on-crime contrast to use against him.
